## Summary

Research confidence is **Low**. Sources do not yet confirm this break's best wind. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- The sources found do not support this break's listed tide preference.
- Limited information is available about which winds are offshore at this break.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- No survey, scientific or official source describes the shape of the bottom.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Re-read 4 of 5 current sources; surfertoday.com returned 403 and is kept unchanged. New readable sources: Surf Atlas Pichilemu (2026), Wavelength (2024) and GoChile (2010, Spanish). Wind remains thin. Only surf-forecast.com gives an offshore direction: ESE (112), within about 23 deg of the profile's 135. WannaSurf lists an S/SE/E wind window and says north winds blow it out, and Wavelength says the cliffs shelter it from the almost daily SW wind. Neither states an offshore direction. Direction: SW (225) from surf-forecast.com and Surf Atlas fits the 210-240 optimum. WannaSurf's N-S list is too broad. Season: Surf Atlas (March-October) matches the profile exactly; surf-forecast.com (winter) and the WSL tour window (April-August) sit inside it. Tide conflict: WannaSurf says low and mid are best, against the profile's 'all'. No other source gives a tide. Size is the main open question. The working ranges are WannaSurf under 3 ft to 16 ft+, Surf Atlas head-high to 25 ft, Wavelength 3-30 ft, WSL 'holds as big as it gets', and GoChile 'from 2 m up'. None confirms the profile's 40 ft maximum, although Wavelength reports 50 ft faces at a 2022 event (a record figure, not recorded). GoChile's 2 m minimum conflicts with WannaSurf and Wavelength (3 ft). Period: only a qualitative 'long-period' (Surf Atlas). No peer-reviewed or official source was found; Crossref returned none, and the Pichilemu municipal culture plan noted in the earlier pass is not in the current source list, so it could not be re-read. The Suston and Carve pages only cover the World Surfing Reserve and were not recorded. A Meteored (2026) article covers Pichilemu generally, citing Chile.Travel, and was not recorded.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | under 3 ft [S3] · 3 ft [S6, S8] · head-high [S5] · 2 m and up [S7] | conflicting | S3, S5, S6, S7, S8 | `wave_height_min_ft` 4 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | 4–10 ft | documented | S6 | no separate setting; working range 4–40 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 20 ft [S8] · 25 ft [S5] · 30 ft [S6] · holds as big as it gets [S4] | conflicting | S3, S4, S5, S6, S8 | `wave_height_max_ft` 40 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working under 1 m / 3 ft, Wavelength and SurferToday (search summary) start at 3 ft, the Surf Atlas at head-high (a face height relative to the surfer), and GoChile says it is surfable from 2 m upward; no source states its scale.
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Starts working at Less than 1m / 3ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S6 (Wavelength Surf Magazine): “It is incredibly consistent, breaking from three feet to 30 feet”
  - S8 (SurferToday): “One guide lists it as a left-hand point break, up to about 800 meters long, best with southwest swells and waves of roughly 3 to 20 feet.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas): “It's the most swell-exposed break in the region, capable of handling waves from head-high to 25 foot.”
  - S7 (GoChile): “pudiendo surfear con olas desde los dos metros hacia arriba por la misma razón que en El Infiernillo”
- **Ideal range**: Wavelength says that between 4 and 10 ft it offers one of the most rippable and bowly waves (a performance range, scale not stated); Wikipedia's 2-3 m is a typical size, not a stated ideal.
  - S6 (Wavelength Surf Magazine): “Between four and 10 feet, it offers one of the most rippable and bowly waves on the planet. As the swell increases, it starts to break out in front of the iconic twin rock pillars.”
- **Maximum suitable**: SurferToday (search summary) gives roughly 3-20 ft, the Surf Atlas head-high to 25 ft, Wavelength 3-30 ft, WSL says it holds as big as it gets, and WannaSurf's 16 ft+ bracket is open-ended; scales are not stated.
  - S8 (SurferToday): “One guide lists it as a left-hand point break, up to about 800 meters long, best with southwest swells and waves of roughly 3 to 20 feet.”
  - S5 (Surf Atlas): “It's the most swell-exposed break in the region, capable of handling waves from head-high to 25 foot.”
  - S6 (Wavelength Surf Magazine): “It is incredibly consistent, breaking from three feet to 30 feet”
  - S4 (World Surf League): “is that it holds as big as it gets”
  - S3 (WannaSurf): “Starts working at Less than 1m / 3ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell height · minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working under 1 m / 3 ft, Wavelength and SurferToday (search summary) start at 3 ft, the Surf Atlas at head-high (a face height relative to the surfer), and GoChile says it is surfable from 2 m upward; no source states its scale.
- **Swell height · maximum suitable**: SurferToday (search summary) gives roughly 3-20 ft, the Surf Atlas head-high to 25 ft, Wavelength 3-30 ft, WSL says it holds as big as it gets, and WannaSurf's 16 ft+ bracket is open-ended; scales are not stated.
